longo.sub: that is how long your raise lasts
longo.nar: You finally got the raise. Ninety days later, your bank account looks exactly the same. That is not bad luck — it is a system, and it has a name.
Economists call it lifestyle creep: every time income rises, spending quietly rises to meet it. The car gets nicer, the apartment gets bigger, the subscriptions multiply.
Here is the anatomy: a rent upgrade takes the first bite, new monthly payments take the second, subscriptions and daily habits split the rest. Within one quarter, the raise is fully absorbed.

longo.sub: of six-figure earners live paycheck to paycheck
longo.cap: Proof it is not about income
longo.nar: And this is the proof it is not about income: nearly half of Americans earning six figures still report living paycheck to paycheck. More money alone has never fixed this.
The only number that builds wealth is the gap: what you earn minus what you spend. A raise that closes the gap makes you richer on paper and poorer in practice.
The defense takes three rules. Pay yourself first. Automate the transfer on payday, before you can touch it. And when income rises, upgrade your lifestyle by half the raise — never all of it.
That last rule is the quiet superpower. Keep half of every raise invested, and your lifestyle still improves — while your gap widens every single year.
Run it forward ten years. The version of you who spent every raise owns a nicer couch. The version who kept half owns assets that pay for the couch.
So the next time a raise disappears, do not blame the salary. Blame the system running underneath it — and remember that systems can be rewritten.

longo.kicker: What would you do with half?
longo.nar: Here is the question: if you kept half of your next raise, where would you put it? Tell us in the comments — and subscribe to see money explained, level by level.

short.nar: Your raise has a lifespan: about ninety days. Then your account looks exactly like before.
Nearly half of six-figure earners live paycheck to paycheck. More money alone fixes nothing.
The fix: pay yourself first, automatically — and keep half of every raise out of your lifestyle.
